strengths: Significance: Accelerating VLA inference without retraining is practically useful. Table 1 reports end-to-end latency reductions from 109 ms to 72.4–78.1 ms across four LIBERO suites, with success rates close to the OpenVLA-OFT baseline. Evaluation on an RTX 3090 provides additional evidence that the speedup is not confined to the A800.

Originality: Combining previous-step attention, current-frame changes, early-layer attention, and action-dependent pruning budgets is a plausible and useful integration. The emphasis on preserving information during precise manipulation provides a robotics-specific motivation beyond generic visual-token pruning.

Soundness: The paper evaluates closed-loop task success rather than relying only on FLOPs or action prediction errors. Table 2 provides initial evidence that static pruning delivers most of the acceleration and that the controller can recover success lost through additional layer pruning.

Presentation and limitations: The overview diagrams and retained-token visualizations make the pipeline understandable. Section 9 appropriately acknowledges the simulation-only evaluation and deployment gap. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility: The central pruning configuration is contradictory. Section 7.1 assigns α=1.0 to Spatial and α=0.6 to Long, whereas Appendix 10.2 reverses these assignments. Section 7.4 and Table 3 indicate that larger α means more pruning, but Algorithm 1 and Appendix 10.2 multiply retained-token budgets by α, implying the opposite direction for those budgets. These differences directly affect the reported accuracy–latency tradeoff and prevent identification of the evaluated configuration.

Methodological specification: Several essential choices remain unresolved, including the dynamic-token budget and similarity threshold, controller velocity thresholds, rank-weight parameter, and precise construction of the previous-step global score. Equation (1) describes attention from visual tokens to text, although the surrounding motivation concerns text attending to visual tokens; the direction and attention mask need clarification. The controller also uses policy-produced displacements without specifying which previous action or action-chunk statistic is available before the current inference. Initialization and treatment of previously pruned token positions are not adequately explained.

Evidence for the proposed mechanisms is insufficient. Table 2 bundles all three static-selection sources together and evaluates only Spatial. It does not isolate temporal attention reuse, dynamic-token supplementation, velocity-based frame selection, or the layer-confidence weighting. There is also no comparison against a fixed pruning budget matched to the controller's average token count. Consequently, the results do not establish that the proposed mechanisms outperform simpler token-selection and budget strategies.

Statistical support and tuning: Reporting 40–50 trials per task without exact counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or paired evaluation details is insufficient to establish negligible degradation or the controller's reported improvement. Differences such as 97.6% versus 98.2% could reflect evaluation variability. Suite-specific pruning ratios are selected for the accuracy–speed tradeoff, but no separate calibration protocol or held-out validation is described.

Baseline comparison: EfficientVLA is reimplemented on a different action-head architecture and includes layer skipping, so its large success-rate loss does not isolate a weakness of its token-selection method. A comparison with layer skipping disabled and accuracy–latency curves under comparable tuning budgets is needed. The main text reports T=112, while the appendix reports 56 retained visual tokens without explaining whether these counts are total or per view. SparseVLM's configuration is also insufficiently documented.

Analytical accuracy and scope: Appendix 10.1 defines M as the number of attention heads in a FLOPs expression that does not correctly account for the backbone's feed-forward computation, and its reduction estimate omits the contribution of the initial full-token layers. This weakens the analytical support, although it does not invalidate measured latency. More broadly, one backbone and one simulation benchmark support a specialized empirical contribution; qualitative two-view examples do not establish the claimed viewpoint-invariant representations. The promising measured gains do not outweigh the unresolved implementation and evidential weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Training-free acceleration of VLA inference is a useful practical objective. Table 1 reports reductions from 109 ms to 72.4–78.1 ms across four LIBERO suites, with success rates close to OpenVLA-OFT. The additional RTX 3090 evaluation supports the usefulness of the implementation across two GPU platforms.

Originality: Combining previous-step attention, current-frame motion, early-layer attention, and action-dependent pruning budgets is a plausible contribution. The action-aware controller provides an interesting connection between computational allocation and manipulation precision.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 40 tasks and includes relevant pruning and caching baselines. Table 2 provides initial evidence that static pruning supplies most of the acceleration and that the controller can recover success rate after additional layer-level pruning.

Presentation and limitations: The overall pipeline and motivating visualizations are understandable. Section 9 appropriately acknowledges the simulation-only evaluation; that honest disclosure is a strength. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility: The pruning configuration is internally inconsistent. Section 7.1 assigns alpha=1.0 to Spatial and 0.6 to Long, whereas Appendix 10.2 reverses these assignments. More fundamentally, Section 7.4 says larger alpha prunes more tokens, consistent with Table 3, but Algorithm 1 and Appendix 10.2 multiply retained-token budgets by alpha, implying the opposite. These contradictions prevent identifying the configuration responsible for the headline results.

Methodological specification: Equation (1) describes attention from visual tokens to text tokens, although the preceding explanation concerns other tokens attending to visual tokens. The exact attention direction and aggregation used for global importance need clarification. The manuscript also omits numerical values for important settings, including motion-similarity and velocity thresholds, the dynamic-token budget, and the rank-weight parameter. The controller uses policy-output displacements to choose pruning before inference, but does not clearly specify which previous action or action-chunk statistic supplies these quantities. These are consequential implementation ambiguities.

Soundness of the accuracy claims: With only 40–50 trials per task, no confidence intervals, and no clearly documented paired evaluation or independent seed runs, the evidence does not establish the claimed negligible accuracy loss or the controller's accuracy improvement. For example, Table 2 changes from 96.8% to 98.2% after adding the controller, but uncertainty is not reported. Suite-specific pruning ratios are selected to balance success and latency without a stated held-out tuning protocol, leaving their generalization uncertain.

Comparative evaluation: The central comparison with EfficientVLA combines aggressive token pruning with removal of four transformer layers. The authors acknowledge that this method was designed for a different action architecture, so its large accuracy loss does not isolate the claimed weakness of local token selection. Matched-budget comparisons and accuracy–latency curves are needed. Table 2 also does not separately ablate previous-step attention, dynamic-token supplementation, early-layer selection, or velocity-based frame sampling, leaving the distinctive contributions insufficiently validated.

Technical analysis: Appendix 10.1's transformer FLOP formula defines M as the number of attention heads but uses 2LDM where the feed-forward network cost should depend on its intermediate width. Its overall reduction formula also fails to include the cost of the two initially unpruned layers correctly. The approximately 63% reduction in the appendix is not reconciled with the 43% remaining FLOPs in Table 1. These problems undermine the analytical support for the efficiency claims, although they do not by themselves invalidate measured latency.

Originality and scope: The work primarily combines existing attention-ranking, temporal-reuse, and adaptive-computation ideas. This can be valuable, but stronger controlled evidence is needed to establish the new understanding contributed by the combination. Experiments use only OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO; running that implementation on two GPUs establishes hardware portability, not generality across VLA architectures. Likewise, qualitative retained-token visualizations do not establish viewpoint-invariant representations as claimed in Section 7.6. Overall, the promising practical result is outweighed by unresolved methodological and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Training-free acceleration of VLA inference is practically useful. Table 1 reports a 1.46× average end-to-end speedup on A800, with success rates within 0.6 percentage points of OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. The additional RTX 3090 evaluation reports 1.57× speedup.
Originality: Combining previous-step attention, current-frame changes, early-layer attention, and action-dependent pruning budgets is a plausible, useful integration of temporal and task information.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 40 tasks, includes relevant pruning and caching baselines, and measures end-to-end latency. Table 2 provides initial evidence that the controller improves the accuracy–latency tradeoff over static and dynamic pruning alone.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline diagrams and retained-token visualizations make the intended method understandable. Section 9 appropriately acknowledges the simulation-only evaluation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially compromised by contradictory pruning configurations. Section 7.1 assigns α=1.0 to Spatial and 0.6 to Long, whereas Appendix 10.2 reverses these settings. More fundamentally, Section 7.4 says larger α prunes more tokens, but Algorithm 1 and Appendix 10.2 multiply retained-token budgets by α, implying the opposite. These inconsistencies prevent identifying the configuration behind the main results.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: dynamic-token budget KD, similarity threshold τ, velocity thresholds, rank-weight parameter k, and the precise layer aggregation used for previous-step global attention. The controller also lacks a clear account of which previously available action supplies its velocity before current inference, including initialization and action-chunk handling. No code-release link is provided.

The attention definition needs clarification. Equation (1) describes attention from visual tokens to instruction tokens, although the intended score measures how instruction tokens attend to visual tokens. Under causal masking with visual tokens preceding instruction tokens, the stated direction would be masked. The paper must specify the actual attention indexing and mask rather than leave this central operation ambiguous.

The evidence does not isolate the main proposed mechanisms. Table 2 bundles previous-step attention, dynamic-image supplementation, and early-layer selection into one static-pruning component, and evaluates ablations only on Spatial. Comparisons against current-only selection and fixed pruning budgets at matched latency are needed to establish the benefits of temporal reuse and action awareness.

Baseline comparisons do not establish a convincing accuracy–latency frontier. EfficientVLA is reimplemented with fixed layer skipping despite its original diffusion-expert setting, and the manuscript gives inconsistent token budgets: 112 in Section 7.2 versus 56 in Appendix 10.2, without explaining whether these are total or per-view counts. Meanwhile, the proposed method uses suite-specific tuning without a reported held-out selection protocol. Matched-budget sweeps would make the comparison substantially stronger.

Statistical support is insufficient for the small accuracy differences and controller gains. The paper reports 40–50 trials per task but provides no exact denominators, confidence intervals, paired-seed analysis, or variability across runs. The point estimates support promising accuracy preservation, but do not establish equivalence or a reliable improvement over the baseline.

The complexity analysis is technically unreliable as written. Appendix 10.1 defines M as the number of attention heads in a 2LDM term, failing to represent the feed-forward intermediate dimension. Its reduction formula also omits the retained cost of the first two full-token layers. The resulting approximately 63% reduction is not reconciled with Table 1's 43% remaining FLOPs. These issues weaken the computational explanation, although they do not by themselves invalidate the measured latency gains.

strengths: Significance: Reducing VLA inference latency without retraining is practically useful. Table 1 reports 1.46× acceleration for OpenVLA-OFT with average success decreasing from 96.6% to 96.1%, and 1.31× for π0 with success decreasing from 94.2% to 93.5%. Additional GPU and physical-robot experiments broaden the evaluation.

Originality: Combining previous-step deep-layer attention, current-step visual changes, and action-dependent token budgets is a useful synthesis. The temporal-overlap measurements provide motivation beyond simply transferring an existing image-token pruning method.

Soundness: Comparisons against several pruning and caching methods, component ablations, and LIBERO-plus perturbation experiments provide encouraging empirical evidence. Tables 2–3 specifically investigate historical attention and entropy weighting.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, with helpful visualizations and substantial appendix material covering hyperparameters, hardware, computational cost, and real-world fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Soundness—central attention definition: Equation 2 explicitly scores visual queries attending to instruction keys, whereas Equation 7 uses text queries attending to image keys. These are different quantities. Under the usual causal OpenVLA-OFT ordering, visual tokens cannot attend to subsequent instruction tokens, making Equation 2 unsuitable as written. The manuscript must specify the actual token ordering, attention mask, and implemented attention direction; this affects essentially every pruning component.

Reproducibility—algorithm specification: Section 5.2 and Appendix A.3 retain 90% of tokens at each pruning stage, but Algorithm 1 retains α×γ%, implying 72% at α=0.8. The handling of first-step initialization, aggregation of middle/deep-layer scores, and token budgets across cameras is also insufficiently specified. Moreover, the stated 15th/32nd-layer selection requires an explanation of its adaptation to π0's different backbone. These ambiguities prevent faithful reconstruction.

Evidence—accuracy preservation is insufficiently quantified: Evaluation episode counts and seed counts are missing. Table 12 reports half-ranges across an unspecified number of runs rather than confidence intervals, and its means differ from the main results without adequate explanation. Physical-robot evaluation likewise lacks trial counts and uncertainty. Table 4 actually shows reductions from 85% to 82% and 91.7% to 90% on two tasks, so the repeated claim of maintaining success without compromise is too strong.

Experimental attribution: The controller ablation increases token retention during selected phases but lacks a fixed-budget comparator with matched average latency or token count, leaving its advantage over simply retaining more tokens unresolved. The adaptive frame-selection mechanism is not separately ablated. EfficientVLA is partially reimplemented at one operating point, limiting conclusions about comparative accuracy–latency trade-offs.

Presentation and measurement consistency: LIBERO-Spatial success at α=0.8 is 97.4% in Table 1 but 97.6% in Table 11. The full-method ablation reports 1.51× speedup versus 1.46× in the principal results without explaining the configuration difference. Timing details such as precision, attention implementation, synchronization, and treatment of first-step entropy computation are insufficiently documented to resolve these discrepancies.

Limitations and generalization: Normalizing action outputs does not establish that velocity thresholds transfer independently of robot kinematics, action scaling, or control frequency. A few trajectory visualizations do not substantiate that broad claim. The manuscript needs a clearer discussion of failures under abrupt scene changes, stale historical importance, and fine manipulation involving upward motion. No material research-ethics violation is evident, but physical-robot safety procedures and the consequences of pruning-induced control failures are not discussed.

strengths: Significance: Training-free VLA acceleration is practically useful. Table 1 reports a favorable operating point: 1.46× speedup with OpenVLA-OFT success decreasing from 96.6% to 96.1%, and 1.31× with π0 decreasing from 94.2% to 93.5%. The additional GPU and real-robot evaluations broaden the evidence beyond FLOP reductions.

Originality: Combining previous-step deep attention, current-step early attention, dynamic image patches, and action-dependent pruning is a plausible contribution. The hierarchical attention and temporal-overlap analyses provide useful motivation, even though the individual ingredients build on established techniques.

Soundness: The paper includes relevant component ablations. Global attention reuse improves reported success from 93.4% to 96.1%, while entropy weighting improves it from 92.0% to 96.1% (Tables 2–3). These results provide preliminary support for the proposed design.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies many thresholds, pruning settings, latency breakdowns, and real-world fine-tuning details. Table 12 also makes an effort to report variation across independent runs.
weaknesses: Soundness—central attention definition: Equation 2 explicitly scores visual queries attending to instruction keys, whereas Equation 7 uses text queries attending to image keys. These are different quantities. For a causal sequence with images preceding instructions, the former attention is masked; the manuscript does not specify token ordering or an attention-mask modification that resolves this issue. The implemented attention direction and head aggregation must be clarified before the central importance estimator can be assessed or reproduced.

Reproducibility—conflicting pruning specifications: Section 5 and Appendix A.3 specify retaining 90% at each dynamic pruning stage, but Algorithm 1 retains αγ, which is 72% at the default α=0.8. Algorithm 1 also updates scores outside pruning layers, whereas Section 5 describes updating and pruning at designated layers. Whether K budgets apply per image or across all images is unclear, making the reported retention counts difficult to reconstruct. The adaptation of the stated layer-15/layer-32 guidance to π0 is also unspecified.

Evidence—accuracy preservation is insufficiently established: Simulation rollout counts, real-world evaluation trial counts, and the number of independent seeds are not provided. Table 12 reports mean ± half-range without enough information to assess uncertainty, and comparable uncertainty is absent for the component ablations. Consequently, the 0.6-percentage-point controller improvement and claims of negligible degradation are difficult to evaluate. Table 4 actually reports declines from 85% to 82% and 91.7% to 90% on two real-world tasks, which should qualify the claim of maintaining success rate.

Experimental controls: The global-reuse ablation changes Klocal from 24 to 54, but local selection unions two layer-specific sets; this does not establish equal retained-token counts or compute. Likewise, the controller preserves more tokens during fine actions, but it is not compared with a fixed policy at matched average compute. The EfficientVLA result uses a partial reimplementation at one operating point. These comparisons support the approach provisionally but do not cleanly isolate its advantages.

Originality and interpretation: The demonstrated novelty is mainly a combination of pruning heuristics. 'Self-speculative' selection has no explicit verification or correction stage, so its relationship to speculative decoding needs sharper qualification. Normalizing actions also does not establish that velocity thresholds transfer independently of robot kinematics, action scaling, or control frequency; the additional trajectory visualization is insufficient to support that broad claim.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: Several inconsistencies reduce confidence in the reporting, including Spatial success of 97.4% versus 97.6% at α=0.8 in Tables 1 and 11, and differing latency figures for apparently corresponding configurations. Limitations concerning stale attention, changing scenes, and velocity-based contact detection receive insufficient discussion. No material ethical violation is evident, but real-robot evaluation would benefit from explicit safety procedures and failure reporting. Overall, the promising efficiency results do not yet overcome the unresolved methodological and evidential issues.

strengths: Significance: Training-free VLA acceleration is practically useful. Table 1 reports 1.46× speedup for OpenVLA-OFT and 1.31× for π0, with average success-rate reductions of 0.5 and 0.7 percentage points. Additional GPU and real-robot evaluations broaden the evidence beyond a single simulated configuration.

Originality: Combining previous-step deep-layer attention, current-step visual changes, early-layer attention, and action-dependent pruning is a useful synthesis. The reported temporal overlap of important tokens provides a plausible motivation for reusing historical attention.

Soundness: The paper includes relevant component ablations. Tables 2 and 3 report benefits from historical attention and entropy weighting, while Figure 8 examines the efficiency–accuracy tradeoff of the three main components.
Presentation: The overall pipeline is understandable, with informative visualizations and an appendix covering several hyperparameters, computational overheads, and real-world fine-tuning settings.
weaknesses: Soundness—central attention definition: Section 4.1.1 and Eq. (2) explicitly use visual queries attending to instruction keys, whereas Section 5.1 and Eq. (7) use text queries attending to visual keys. These are different quantities. Under the standard causal OpenVLA-OFT sequence arrangement, visual tokens cannot attend to subsequent instruction tokens, making Eq. (2) particularly problematic. The actual attention direction, token order, and masking must be specified; otherwise the central selection mechanism cannot be reliably reproduced.

Reproducibility—conflicting pruning rules: Section 5.2 and Appendix A.3 retain 90% of tokens at each dynamic pruning stage, but Algorithm 1 retains α × γ%, implying 72% at the default α=0.8. The manuscript also does not clearly specify how top-K budgets are allocated across cameras and guiding layers, how historical token identities are maintained after pruning, or how the 32-layer recipe is adapted to π0. These ambiguities materially affect both accuracy and computation.

Evidence for accuracy preservation is insufficiently quantified. Evaluation trial counts are not specified for the main simulation or real-world results. Table 12 reports mean ± half-range over an unspecified number of seeds, which does not establish statistical uncertainty or equivalence. Table 4 shows real-world declines from 85.0% to 82.0% and from 91.7% to 90.0%; the conclusion's claim of speedup 'without compromising success rate' is stronger than this evidence supports.

Comparative evaluation and timing need stronger controls. EfficientVLA is only partially reimplemented, and the manuscript compares individual operating points rather than matched success-rate/latency curves. The global-attention ablation changes candidate sources without demonstrating equal realized token counts after unions. Timing details such as inference precision, attention backend, synchronization, warm-up, and treatment of first-step overhead are missing, limiting confidence in reproducibility of the speedups.

Originality and limitations: The contribution is primarily a combination of pruning heuristics, and 'self-speculative' does not include the verification mechanism associated with speculative decoding. Claims that normalized velocity thresholds generalize independently of robot kinematics and environmental scaling are insufficiently supported by trajectory examples and limited platform tests. Abrupt scene changes, historical-attention errors, and fine manipulation involving upward motion deserve explicit limitations and targeted evaluation. I found no material research-ethics concern, but the unresolved methodological and evidential issues prevent acceptance.
